name: Automatic Task Helper
intro: A desktop tool for turning repetitive browser work into reusable, understandable workflows.
overview: Automatic Task Helper started with a very specific frustration: applying for jobs meant repeatedly navigating different application sites, entering the same information, and performing nearly identical browser actions. The first instinct was effectively to build a better job-application automator. Instead of tying the solution to one site or one application flow, the project evolved toward a more general question: could the repetitive browser actions themselves become reusable building blocks?

That shift turned the project into a Python desktop application for constructing browser-action queues. A user can define navigation, clicks, text input, delays, repeats, bulk operations, fallbacks, and conditional actions; preview which page elements a step will target; save the resulting workflow; and run it again later. What began as personal job-search automation became a general-purpose browser workflow tool that is functional for personal use while its remaining work is increasingly about hardening and productization rather than proving the core concept.
challenge: Let people automate fragile browser tasks while keeping every step visible enough to understand, adjust, and trust.
approach: Treat browser work as a sequence of observable actions, then give an agent enough context to help build and recover those sequences without hiding what it is doing.

highlights.title: Reusable queues
highlights.text: Capture a routine once, then run the same sequence again when the work returns.

highlights.title: Human-readable steps
highlights.text: Clicks, entries, waits, and checks stay visible instead of disappearing into code.

highlights.title: Built for the messy web
highlights.text: Conditional steps help workflows handle pages that do not behave exactly the same every time.

next: Improve workflow recovery and make building a first automation faster.
